Downtown & The Flats 42 places · area 1 of 4

  1. 1 Must see within Downtown & The Flats

    Chess Collection — Cleveland Public Library MAIN Library

    This is the right building. The 1925 Main Library on Superior Avenue — not a branch, not the Louis Stokes Wing next door. Go in the Main Building, take the marble staircase to the third floor, and pass through the John Griswold White Exhibition Corridor (look for owls in the wrought-iron cases) into Special Collections.

    Inside is the John G. White Chess and Checkers Collection: the largest chess collection in the world. Over 35,000 items going back to the 12th century — one-of-a-kind sets from every continent, rare manuscripts, Bobby Fischer score sheets, Lasker medals, the most comprehensive tournament records anywhere, and two death masks of Gisela Kahn Gresser, nine-time US women's champion. White was a Cleveland attorney who collected from 1870 until his death in 1928, buying up entire European and American chess libraries; the library has kept collecting since. It has been on this floor since the doors opened.

    Your guide’s note Bring photo ID such as a driving licence. It is a closed research collection — you request items and are shown one at a time, so email special.collections@cpl.org ahead if you want something specific pulled. Closed Sunday.

    Note: News 5's list prints the address as 525 Superior. That is wrong — the Main Library is at 325 Superior Ave.

    325 Superior Ave NE · Main Building, 3rd floor, John G. White Special Collections

    Recommended by ,

  2. 2 Must see within Downtown & The Flats

    The Arcade (Old Arcade)

    Five-story glass-roofed atrium built in 1890 as America's first indoor shopping centre, modelled on Milan's Galleria and financed in part by Rockefeller. Top three floors are now a Hyatt. A Superman film was shot here.

    Your guide’s note Stand at the far end and look up the full height. Grab Pizza 216 while you're in.

    401 Euclid Ave

    Recommended by ,

  3. 3 Must see within Downtown & The Flats

    Terminal Tower Observation Deck

    The 42nd floor of a 52-story tower that was briefly the world's second-tallest. Views across the bridges, the Cuyahoga and Lake Erie. Small and dated in a way that's part of the appeal.

    Your guide’s note Book online in advance — no walk-ups. Check in at the ground-floor desk, ride to 32, transfer to 42. Around $5–6. Weekends only.

    50 Public Square, 42nd floor

    Recommended by ,

    Soldiers' & Sailors' Monument

    Civil War memorial with a free museum inside — bronze reliefs, marble busts, knowledgeable volunteers. Beneath it runs a labyrinth of tunnels that opens to the public one day a year.

    Your guide’s note Ask at the desk whether a tunnel tour is scheduled. Interior alone: 20–30 minutes. Free.

    3 Public Square

    Rock & Roll Hall of Fame

  7. 7 Must see within Downtown & The Flats

    GE Chandelier, Playhouse Square

    The largest outdoor chandelier in North America, hung 44 feet above Euclid Avenue: 4,200 crystals, each placed by hand at roughly twenty minutes apiece. It anchors Playhouse Square, the largest performing arts centre in the United States outside Lincoln Center — five restored 1920s theatres saved from demolition by a volunteer campaign.

    Your guide’s note Free and lit every night. Go after dark. Parking nearby is genuinely difficult.

    E 14th St at Euclid Ave

    Recommended by , Added by the guide (general knowledge)

    Steamship William G. Mather

    A 618-foot Great Lakes freighter tied up beside the Science Center, open stem to stern — engine room, pilot house, crew quarters and the panelled guest staterooms. The deck gives one of the better skyline views in the city.

    Your guide’s note Closed Monday, and seasonal. Included with Great Lakes Science Center membership.

    601 Erieside Ave, North Coast Harbor

  10. 10 Must see within Downtown & The Flats

    Hope Memorial Bridge & the Guardians of Traffic

    Eight art deco sandstone giants, each 43 feet tall, holding vehicles from a hay wagon to a 1930s truck — Henry Hering's Guardians of Traffic, carved into the bridge pylons in 1932. The baseball team took its name from them. Pedestrian walkways run both sides.

    Your guide’s note Walk it rather than drive it. Best light is late afternoon from the west end.

    Hope Memorial Bridge, over the Cuyahoga

    Recommended by Added by the guide (general knowledge)

  15. 15 Worth the detour within Downtown & The Flats

    Jesse Owens Statue

    William McVey's 1982 bronze. Owens was born in Alabama and died in Arizona, but he spent his formative years in Cleveland before winning four golds at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — in front of a regime whose entire racial theory he demolished in a week.

    Fort Huntington Park, 299 W Lakeside Ave

  16. 16 Worth the detour within Downtown & The Flats

    USS Cod Submarine Memorial

    The last fully intact WWII fleet submarine in existence. No cut-away hull, no visitor stairs — you go in the way the crew did. Veterans narrate in person; push-button stations cover the rest.

    Your guide’s note Entry is down a vertical ladder through a deck hatch. Not accessible, and genuinely tight. Seasonal — confirm before driving out.

    1201 N Marginal Rd

University Circle & East Side 59 places · area 2 of 4

  1. 1 Must see within University Circle & East Side

    Haserot Angel, Lake View Cemetery

    Formally "The Angel of Death Victorious." A life-size bronze on the Haserot family plot, holding an extinguished torch upside down. Decades of oxidation have left black streaks running from her eyes down her neck, so she appears to weep. Herman Matzen sculpted her; canning magnate Francis Haserot commissioned her after his wife died in 1919.

    Your guide’s note Easy to miss — just off the road under trees. Grab a map at the gate; nearest marked landmark is the Hanna Mausoleum.

    12316 Euclid Ave · Section 9, Lot 14

    Recommended by , ,

  2. 2 Must see within University Circle & East Side · Vietnamese

    Superior Phở

    Vietnamese-owned and family-run in Asiatown, and by consensus the best phở in the city. The bone broth simmers 24 hours from a recipe passed down through the family; the owner is known to throw out an entire vat that doesn't meet standard. Fourteen versions of phở, plus bánh mì, bún thịt nướng, summer rolls and proper Vietnamese coffee.

    Your guide’s note Enter through Golden Plaza, a nondescript mini-mall with free parking. Closed Monday. Do not confuse it with Number One Pho two doors down — people mix them up constantly.

    3030 Superior Ave E #105, Asiatown

    Recommended by , ,

  3. 3 Must see within University Circle & East Side · Chinese

    Li Wah — Cantonese dim sum carts

    Cantonese. Freshwater calls it the best dim sum in Cleveland and it is still the only place running proper steel carts at weekend lunch — har gow, siu mai, chicken feet, roast duck, rice rolls, circling the room. Hundreds of people pack it on Saturday and Sunday.

    Your guide’s note Carts run weekend lunch only; come before 1pm or you get the menu instead. Some off-cart dishes draw mixed reviews — stick to dim sum and roast meats.

    Asia Plaza, 2999 Payne Ave #102

    Recommended by , ,

  4. 4 Must see within University Circle & East Side

    Percy Skuy Collection, Dittrick Medical History Center

    The largest and most comprehensive collection of historical contraceptives in the world — over a thousand objects arranged chronologically across a millennium. Beaver testicles, crocodile dung, mule earwax, spider carcasses, Mexican yams, Goodyear rubbers, IUDs. Alongside sit the texts: Casanova recommending a hollowed half-lemon, and 1580 BCE instructions involving ground dates, acacia and honey. The wider Dittrick galleries on medical history are excellent in their own right.

    Your guide’s note Very limited hours and they should drive your whole day. Free. Metered street parking.

    11000 Euclid Ave, Allen Memorial Medical Library

    Recommended by ,

  5. 5 Must see within University Circle & East Side

    Lake View Cemetery (whole grounds)

    280 acres, 100,000 graves, and the best architecture walk in the city: the James A. Garfield Memorial and tomb, Wade Memorial Chapel with a Louis Tiffany interior, and mausoleums throughout. Climb the Garfield tower for a downtown view.

    Your guide’s note Maps at the gate, main office and Garfield Monument. Bikes allowed. A trolley tour runs at 1pm — call to book. Open every day of the year.

    12316 Euclid Ave

    Recommended by ,

    Wonton Gourmet & BBQ

    Cantonese / Hong Kong-style. Freshwater rates it the best Chinese restaurant in Asiatown and says some would extend that to all of Northeast Ohio. Roast duck and char siu hanging in the window, chive pot stickers, shrimp wonton noodle soup, three-flavour dumpling soup, salt-baked shrimp, soy sauce chicken, beef chow fun. Full-colour photos of nearly every dish cover three of the four walls.

    Your guide’s note Closed Tuesday. Cash-friendly, cheap, and not remotely fancy.

    3211 Payne Ave, Asiatown

    Recommended by ,

    Your guide’s note Enter via Wade Park and the South entrance for the approach across the lagoon. Special exhibitions are ticketed; the permanent collection isn't. Closed Monday.

  8. 8 Must see within University Circle & East Side

    Lucy, at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History

    The Australopithecus afarensis skeleton — the oldest discovered link in the chain of human evolution, and Cleveland's most famous resident. Balto the sled dog is here too, taxidermied and on display. Live animals outside, including a bald eagle.

    Your guide’s note Planetarium and 3D films cost extra. Attached garage. Two hours minimum. Closed Monday.

    1 Wade Oval Dr

    Recommended by

    Quintana's Speakeasy

    Go to the back door of the barbershop and spa. Press the buzzer. Say you're there to see a man about a horse. Up the stairs, turn right, find the bookshelf, pull the correct book — the wall opens onto a 1920s bar.

    Your guide’s note Closed Sunday and Monday. Small capacity; the attic room is the quiet one. They run cocktail classes.

    2200 S Taylor Rd, Cleveland Heights

    Recommended by

  10. 10 Must see within University Circle & East Side

    Wade Memorial Chapel

    From outside, an unremarkable cemetery chapel. Inside, a Louis Tiffany interior: a monumental stained-glass window and glass mosaic murals running the length of both walls, executed by an all-female workshop. It was the first place in Cleveland outside a private home to have electric light. The bronze doors weigh two tons and swing on a finger.

    Your guide’s note Open daily 10–4, free, and there is usually a volunteer docent inside who will tell you far more than any placard. Do this in the same visit as the Haserot Angel and Garfield's tomb.

    Lake View Cemetery, 12316 Euclid Ave

    Recommended by

    The Thinker

    A Rodin cast at the museum's south entrance, and one of very few in the world deliberately left damaged. A bomb detonated at its base in 1970 — attributed to the Weather Underground — tore off the lower legs and pedestal. The museum chose not to restore it.

    Cleveland Museum of Art, 11150 East Blvd

West Side, Ohio City & Tremont 52 places · area 3 of 4

  1. 1 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont

    West Side Market

    A hundred stalls under a 1912 barrel-vaulted hall with a clock tower — butchers, bakers, fishmongers, cheesemongers, spice sellers. Kielbasa in every form: smoked, fresh, double-smoked, Hungarian, Polish. One stand is called the Pork Chop Shop. Food has been sold on or beside this site since 1840. Look for the steer's head carved into the northern pediment, and go up to the balcony for the view down the hall.

    Your guide’s note Bring cash — most stalls don't take cards. First hour of parking free; park toward the back near the beer garden. The outdoor produce arcade is a separate building and a harder sell than the main hall. Closed Tuesday and Thursday.

    1979 W 25th St, Ohio City

    Recommended by , ,

  2. 2 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont

    Buckland Museum of Witchcraft & Magick

    Raymond Buckland — leader of what became the Long Island Coven — started this collection in a Bay Shore basement in the 1960s. It followed him to New Hampshire, through legal disputes in New Orleans, into storage in Columbus, and finally here. Much of it originally belonged to Gerald Gardner, father of Gardnerian Wicca, including his besom. Also: Sybil Leek's crystal ball, Egyptian ushabtis, a carved mandrake root, Crowley material, rare Ouija memorabilia, and a demon in a box that Buckland captured in the 1970s with help from a ceremonial magician.

    Your guide’s note Ten minutes from downtown. Parking behind the building and on the street. Photos without flash; the curator asks for no video. Small enough for an hour, dense enough to want longer.

    2155 Broadview Rd

    Recommended by ,

  3. 3 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont

    A Christmas Story House & Museum

    The actual exterior house from the 1983 film, restored inside to match the movie, plus a museum of original props and costumes across the street. The tour covers why it was shot in Cleveland at all.

    Your guide’s note House interior is tour-only; tickets at the gift shop, departures every 30 minutes from 10:15am. Budget two hours. You can rent the house and sleep in Ralphie's bedroom.

    3159 W 11th St, Tremont

    Recommended by ,

  4. 4 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont · Unique American

    Market Garden Brewery

    Sam McNulty's Ohio City anchor brewery (2011), right across from the West Side Market — a 320-seat brewpub with a 3,000-sq-ft American beer garden, three fireplaces, and a rooftop patio, plus a full production brewhouse. A cornerstone of Ohio City's Brewing District and a regular on Cleveland Magazine's best-breweries guide.

    1947 W 25th St, Cleveland, OH 44113

    Recommended by ,

  5. 5 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont

    St. Theodosius Russian Orthodox Cathedral

    Onion domes over Tremont, and the church from The Deer Hunter. Icons, stained glass, permanent incense. If you see only one of Tremont's churches, this is it.

    Your guide’s note Weekday mornings and around services. Tremont is dense with immigrant-built churches — walk the neighbourhood for the rest.

    733 Starkweather Ave, Tremont

    Recommended by

  6. 6 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont

    The Sanctuary Museum (Museum of Divine Statues)

    Makeup artist Lou McClung spent years rescuing statues, stained glass, altarpieces and relics from Catholic parishes across the Diocese of Cleveland as they closed, then restoring them. The result is a room of hundreds of saved objects that would otherwise have been landfilled. The wall of relics is the centrepiece — step too close and you trip the laser.

    Your guide’s note The hardest schedule on this list: two short windows a week. Small admission. Call ahead.

    12905 Madison Ave, Lakewood

    Recommended by

  7. 7 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont

    Solstice Steps, Lakewood Park

    Terraced stone steps down to Lake Erie, built so everyone gets a front-row seat rather than a handful of benches. Best sunset in the region, with the skyline visible east. Porch swings on the bluff.

    Your guide’s note Arrive 30 minutes before sunset for a seat on the lower terraces. Windy and cold well into spring.

    14532 Lake Ave, Lakewood

    Recommended by

  8. 8 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont

    Franklin Castle

    The Hannes Tiedemann house, 1881 — a Victorian sandstone pile with a history of family deaths and a reputation as the most haunted house in Ohio. Atlas Obscura has its own entry for it; your four links were only a fraction of what they list for Cleveland.

    Your guide’s note Interior access is by booked tour or overnight stay only, currently Tuesday evenings. The exterior and the surrounding Franklin Boulevard mansions are free to walk.

    4308 Franklin Blvd, Ohio City

  12. 12 Must see within West Side, Ohio City & Tremont · Singaporean

    Dang Good Foods

    The only Singaporean kitchen I can find in Cleveland, and it passes the test. Confirmed on the menu: chai tow kway (white carrot cake, which they will make Singapore-spicy if you ask), curry laksa, roti, and pork bao — Hokkien and Teochew dishes cooked as dishes, not as an idea of Singapore. Three house chilli oils. A diner who lived in Singapore ten years went specifically to test it and stayed.

    Your guide’s note Closed Sunday and Monday; dinner-only most nights (4:30–9), Friday from noon, Saturday 12–3 then 4:30–8:30. Small room — call ahead.

    Honest caveat: I could not confirm char kway teow or Hainanese chicken rice on the current menu, and the menu is short and rotates. Ask when you call. What I can confirm is that there is no “Singapore noodles” nonsense here.

    13735 Madison Ave, Lakewood

  1. 1 Must see within Suburbs, Metroparks & Day Trips

    Brandywine Falls

    A 65-foot waterfall reached by a boardwalk from the car park, viewable from above or from the gorge floor. Different in every season.

    Your guide’s note Stairs at both viewing levels — not fully accessible. Gets very busy; go early.

  3. 3 Must see within Suburbs, Metroparks & Day Trips

    Beck Center for the Arts

    The largest performing-arts and arts-education center on Cleveland's West Shore — a nonprofit founded in 1931 (as Lakewood Little Theatre) that entertains and educates 65,000+ people a year across two stages on a 3.5-acre Detroit Ave campus. Professional theater, galleries, and classes; documented by the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History and listed by TourismOhio.

    17801 Detroit Ave, Lakewood, OH 44107

    Recommended by ,

  4. 4 Must see within Suburbs, Metroparks & Day Trips

    Rocky River Reservation & Fort Hill Stairs

    A Cleveland Metroparks jewel of the Emerald Necklace winding along the Rocky River — over five miles of trails to river's edge, wetlands, ponds and ancient Native American earthworks, plus the Fort Hill Stairs (155 steps rising 90 ft to a bluff-top view). The Rocky River Nature Center displays the prehistoric fish Dunkleosteus and the kid-favorite HideAway Hollow oak.

    24000 Valley Pkwy, North Olmsted, OH 44070

    Recommended by ,

  5. 5 Must see within Suburbs, Metroparks & Day Trips

    Huntington Reservation & Beach

    A ~100-acre Cleveland Metroparks lakefront reservation in Bay Village with a swimming beach on Lake Erie, three miles of trails through beach-forest-meadow habitats, and the landmark 1927 Huntington water tower with a play space and snack spot. Home to two Metroparks affiliates (Lake Erie Nature & Science Center and BAYarts).

    Lake Rd at Wolf Rd, Bay Village, OH 44140

  6. 6 Must see within Suburbs, Metroparks & Day Trips

    Cain Park

    One of the oldest municipally owned arts parks in the U.S., conceived in 1938 by Heights drama teacher Dr. Dina Rees Evans and Mayor Frank C. Cain — the covered 2,782-seat Evans Amphitheater, the Alma Theater, the Feinberg gallery, and the July Cain Park Arts Festival, a nationally top-rated juried outdoor art fair. Entrances at Lee Rd and Superior Park Dr.

    14591 Superior Rd, Cleveland Heights, OH 44118

How we choose

Every place is recommended by named sources (Yelp and TripAdvisor never count as the recommender), pinned to its door from a published coordinate, and status-checked. Closed places stay, flagged, so you know they’re gone.

Must see
The places to plan a visit around — graded within each area, not across the city.
Worth the detour
Strong picks, worth going out of your way for.
Deep cut
For the curious: smaller, odder, more local.

Within each area, places are ordered by tier, then by number of named sources — never by popularity. Numbers on the cards match the pins on the map. No ratings, prices or opening hours are shown, because the guide doesn’t hold verified ones.

How this guide was made

How the cuisine filters were policed

Vietnamese — only Vietnamese-owned or Vietnamese-family kitchens named by local press. Singaporean — the menu had to carry actual Singaporean dishes; “Singapore noodles” would have disqualified a place, and Cleveland has exactly one that passes. Chinese — the regional tradition is stated on each card (Cantonese, Sichuan) and only places raved about by Cleveland Scene, Cleveland Magazine or Freshwater are here. Unique American, European, Latin American — had to be viral or heavily raved, no generic burger or pizza. Middle Eastern — you asked specifically about Persian; there is no Persian restaurant in Cleveland with that reputation, so I have said so on the card rather than padding the list. Two Bourdain restaurants are included even though they are permanently closed, so you know they are gone rather than hunting for them.

What the web turned up

Most Cleveland "hidden gems" listicles online are recycled SEO with no local reporting, so I did not use them. The one genuinely useful find was that Atlas Obscura catalogues around 33 Cleveland places — your four links were a fraction of it — so the rest are now included and tagged ATLAS OBSCURA. Everything tagged ADDED is from my own knowledge rather than a specific article: places locals treat as essential that the hidden-gem lists skip precisely because they are not hidden.
